a: Ecbatana
p: Ecbatana, today Hamadan in western Iran, was the old capital of the Medes and later a royal summer seat.
b: Ecbatana (modern Hamadan) lay on the high plateau of Media, about 450 miles east of Nineveh by road. It had been the capital of the Medes, and the Persian kings later kept a palace and archive there: Ezra 6:2 says Cyrus's decree for the Temple was found in the fortress at Ecbatana. In Tobit it is the home of Raguel's family, and in 14:12–13 it becomes the safe home of Tobias's household when Nineveh falls. Rages, where Gabael lives (9:2), lay farther east, near modern Tehran.

a: the ones carried off as captives to Nineveh
p: Tobit's tribe, Naphtali, was the first in the north to be deported by the Assyrians.
b: Tobit belongs to Naphtali, a northern tribe (1:1–2). The book of Kings says the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III took the people of Naphtali captive to Assyria about 733 BC (2 Kings 15:29), and Samaria fell about 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6). Tobit 1:2 dates Tobit's own exile to "Enemessar," that is, Shalmaneser. The story imagines a family of the "lost" northern tribes still keeping faith in Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, and finding kin as far away as Media, where 2 Kings 17:6 also places exiles.

a: a righteous man who gave alms has gone blind
t: The book's question in Raguel's mouth
p: Raguel says aloud what the reader has wondered since chapter 2: why does a good man suffer?
b: Tobit went blind after burying a murdered kinsman (2:3–10). Raguel's cry names the puzzle that the book shares with Job and Psalm 73: righteousness and generosity do not protect a person from disaster. Tobit does not answer with an argument. It answers with a story: God has already heard the prayer (3:16–17), and the angel is sitting at Raguel's table. Readers who know this are meant to feel the irony, and to learn to trust a care they cannot see (see 12:14).

a: since you are my closest kin
t: The nearest kinsman's right to marry
p: Tobit says the law of Moses gives Tobias the first right to Sarah. The 66 books contain no such law.
b: Raguel, like Raphael in 6:12–13, says the closest relative has the right to marry an only daughter, and calls this "the ruling written in the book of Moses" (7:11–12). Agrees in part: Numbers 36:6–9 says daughters who inherit their father's land must marry within their father's tribe, so that the land stays in the tribe, and Numbers 27:8 lets daughters inherit when there is no son. Ruth 3:12–13 and 4:1–10 show a closer relative having first claim. Goes beyond: no law in the five books of Moses gives the nearest kinsman the right to marry an heiress, and none sets death for a father who refuses (6:13). Scholars think Tobit reads custom and the spirit of Numbers 36 as Moses' ruling. The marriage of close kin is the subject of the card at chapter 4.

a: Heaven has decided that you should have her
p: "Heaven" here is a respectful way to say God. The match was settled above before it was arranged below.
b: The Greek is ek tou ouranou kekritai, "it has been judged from heaven." Jews of this period often said "heaven" instead of naming God (Daniel 4:26; Luke 15:18; Matthew 21:25). Raphael has already said that Sarah was set apart for Tobias "before the ages" (6:18). The later rabbis said something similar: forty days before a child is formed, a voice from heaven announces whom he will marry (Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 2a). Tobit is an early witness to that belief in marriages made in heaven.
orig: ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ κέκριταί σοι δοθῆναι (ek tou ouranou kekritai soi dothēnai), 'it has been judged from heaven that she be given to you'

a: From this moment you are her brother and she is your sister
p: Raguel speaks the words that made a marriage, much like formulas in Jewish marriage contracts from the 400s BC.
b: Ancient Near Eastern marriages were made by a spoken declaration and often a written contract (7:13). Aramaic marriage documents from the Jewish colony at Elephantine in Egypt, from the 400s BC, contain the groom's words, "She is my wife and I am her husband from this day and forever." Hosea 2:2 turns the same kind of formula around for a divorce: "She is not my wife, and I am not her husband." Raguel's version uses "brother" and "sister," the language of kinship and love in Tobit (see 7:15), and adds "from today for all time."

a: Taking her by the hand, he handed her over to Tobias
p: The father gives the bride, as Laban and Bethuel gave Rebekah. The whole scene echoes Genesis 24 and 29.
b: Tobit tells Tobias's journey for a bride in the shape of the patriarchs' stories. A servant (here an angel in disguise) guides the young man to the family; the bride's family welcomes him with tears and kisses, as Laban welcomed Jacob (Genesis 29:11–13); and the father hands the bride over: "Here is Rebekah in front of you. Take her and go" (Genesis 24:51). The first readers, who knew Genesis well, would hear that God is guiding this family as he guided Abraham's.

a: a marriage contract
t: The first written marriage contract in a biblical story
p: The Greek calls it a "document of living together." Jews later called such a contract a ketubah.
b: The Greek syngraphē biblíou synoikēseōs means a written contract of marriage. No marriage in the 66 books is said to be put in writing, though divorce papers are (Deuteronomy 24:1). Real Jewish marriage contracts survive from Elephantine in Egypt in the 400s BC, and later Jewish law required a written ketubah listing what the husband owes his wife (Mishnah Ketubot). The Vaticanus text adds that the contract was sealed. Tobit is an early literary witness to the custom.
orig: συνγραφὴν βιβλίου συνοικήσεως (syngraphēn bibliou synoikēseōs)

a: Sister
p: Husbands and wives call each other "brother" and "sister" in Tobit, as lovers do in the Song of Songs.
b: Raguel calls his wife "sister" (adelphē), Tobit calls Anna "sister" (10:6), and Tobias calls Sarah "sister" on their wedding night (8:4, 8:7). Everyone in the book also calls kinsmen and fellow Israelites "brother." The words mark marriage as a bond of kin and affection, not ownership. The Song of Songs uses the same language: "my sister, my bride" (Song of Songs 4:9–12), and Egyptian love poetry does too. The Plain keeps the words, since the book's warm family language depends on them.
orig: Ἀδελφή (adelphē), 'sister'

a: gladness instead of your grief
p: Edna's blessing uses a prophetic hope: God turns mourning into joy.
b: Sarah prayed in 3:10–15 to die rather than hear more insults. Her mother now prays the reversal the prophets promised: "I will turn their mourning into joy" (Jeremiah 31:13), "the oil of gladness instead of mourning" (Isaiah 61:3), "My mourning song you changed into a dance for me" (Psalm 30:11). Jesus uses the same pattern: "your grief will become joy" (John 16:20). By 8:16–17 the prayer is answered.

a: laid them on the ashes of the incense
p: Burning things to drive off demons was common in the ancient world. Tobit puts it under God's instruction.
b: Mesopotamian healing and exorcism texts often prescribe fumigation: burning plants, hair or animal parts to drive an evil spirit away. Tobit's fish liver and heart (6:7, 6:17) belong to that world. Verdict: the link is real at the level of folk medicine, but the book frames it differently: the remedy is an angel's instruction, and Tobias and Sarah must still pray (6:18; 8:4–8). The demon flees from the smell, but it is Raphael who binds it (8:3). Churches that read Tobit differ on what the episode teaches about exorcism; see the card at chapter 6.

a: it fled up into the regions of Egypt
p: Sinaiticus says "up into the regions of Egypt"; Vaticanus says "the uppermost parts of Egypt"; the Vulgate, "the desert of upper Egypt."
b: The Sinaiticus Greek is anō eis ta merē Aigyptou, "up into the parts of Egypt." Vaticanus has "to the uppermost (parts) of Egypt," which may mean Upper Egypt in the far south. Jerome's Latin reads "in the desert of upper Egypt." Egypt was famous for magic, and Jews pictured demons living in deserts and ruins (Isaiah 13:21; Isaiah 34:14; Matthew 12:43). Either way, the point is that the demon is driven as far as possible from Sarah.
orig: ἄνω εἰς τὰ μέρη Αἰγύπτου (anō eis ta merē Aigyptou); Vaticanus εἰς τὰ ἀνώτατα Αἰγύπτου

a: he shackled its feet and bound it fast
p: In 1 Enoch an angel named Raphael binds Azazel hand and foot. Revelation pictures an angel binding the dragon.
b: In the Book of the Watchers God tells Raphael to "bind Azazel hand and foot" and throw him into darkness in the desert (1 Enoch 10:4–5). Tobit shares that tradition: Raphael, "God heals," is the angel who binds evil spirits. Revelation 20:2 shows an angel seizing the dragon and binding him, and Jesus speaks of tying up the strong man before plundering his house (Mark 3:27). The Christian imagination of a healing angel who also binds the devil draws on this scene.

a: Let us pray and plead with our Lord
t: The Vulgate's three nights of prayer
p: In Jerome's Latin, Tobias and Sarah keep three nights of prayer before living as husband and wife.
b: The Greek has one prayer, then sleep (8:9). Jerome's Vulgate is different. There Raphael tells Tobias to keep apart from Sarah for three days and give himself only to prayer with her (Vulgate 6:18–22), and Tobias says, "Sara, exsurge, et deprecemur Deum hodie, et cras, et secundum cras": "Sara, arise, and let us pray to God to day, and to morrow, and the next day" (Douay 8:4), "for we are the children of saints" (Douay 8:5). Because the Vulgate was the Western church's Bible for a thousand years, these "Tobias nights" shaped Catholic marriage teaching and custom; see the card on this chapter.

a: Blessed are you, God of our fathers
p: "Blessed are you" is the form of Jewish prayer that later became the berakhah of the synagogue.
b: Almost every prayer in Tobit begins "Blessed are you" or "Blessed be God" (3:11; 8:5; 8:15; 11:14; 13:1). The Greek eulogētos ei stands for Hebrew barukh attah, the opening of the blessings (berakhot) that Jews still say. The Prayer of Azariah in the Additions to Daniel begins the same way (Daniel 3:26 in the Greek). Tobit shows the pattern already in use around 200 BC, before the rabbis fixed the wording of the daily prayers.

a: Let us make him a helper like him
p: Tobias quotes Genesis 2:18 as the Greek Old Testament has it: "let us make," not "I will make."
b: Tobias grounds his marriage in creation. His quotation follows the Septuagint of Genesis 2:18, where God says "let us make" (poiēsōmen) and the helper is "like him" (homoion autō; the Septuagint of Genesis has kat' auton, "corresponding to him"). The Hebrew has "I will make," and the site's Plain reads, "It is not good for the man to be by himself" (Genesis 2:18), with a helper "who is his match." Jesus also roots marriage in Genesis 1–2 (Mark 10:6–9). Tobias's prayer is the oldest known Jewish wedding prayer built on that text.
orig: ποιήσωμεν αὐτῷ βοηθὸν ὅμοιον αὐτῷ (poiēsōmen autō boēthon homoion autō)

a: a helper to lean on
p: Tobit adds a word Genesis does not have: Eve was a stērigma, something to lean on.
b: The Greek pairs boēthos, "helper," the word the Greek Genesis uses, with stērigma, "prop, support, something that holds up." In the Bible "helper" is no lowly word: God is Israel's helper (Psalm 33:20; Psalm 121:1–2). Tobit's added word makes the wife a source of strength, not a servant. Vaticanus puts the words in a different order (βοηθὸν Εὕαν στήριγμα, "Eve as a helper, a support") but keeps both.
orig: βοηθὸν στήριγμα (boēthon stērigma)

a: not for sexual immorality, but in truth
p: What is Tobias denying? Lust, a wrong kind of marriage, or both?
b: Porneia usually means sexual immorality. Readers take Tobias's words in three ways. (1) Not for lust: he marries out of love and faithfulness, not desire alone; so the KJV ("not for lust") and Jerome ("not for fleshly lust," with "only for the love of posterity," Douay 8:9). (2) Not a wrong marriage: in 4:12 Tobit links porneia with marrying outside one's own people, so Tobias may mean that this is the right, lawful marriage. (3) "In truth" (ep' alētheias) may mean sincerely, or in keeping with God's law. The readings can stand together.
orig: οὐχὶ διὰ πορνίαν ἐγὼ λαμβάνω (ouchi dia pornian egō lambanō)

a: let us grow old side by side
p: Tobias's last request is simple: a long life together. By 14:12–14 it is granted.
b: The verb synkatagērasai, "to grow old together," is found nowhere else in the Greek Old Testament. Sinaiticus adds koinōs, "together," and the same word returns in 8:13, where the maid finds the two "side by side," alive. Psalm 128:3–6 pictures the blessed man's wife and children around his table and grandchildren in his old age; Ecclesiastes 9:9 tells a man to enjoy life with the wife he loves. Christians still pray Tobias's words at weddings.

a: dug a grave
p: While the couple sleeps, Raguel is out digging a grave. Many readers find the scene meant to be funny.
b: Tobit is serious about God, but it is also a well-told story with humor. Raguel celebrates the wedding and then quietly digs a grave, sends a maid with a lamp, and finally has the grave filled in before dawn so the neighbors never know (8:18). Literary readers see irony: the reader knows the demon is bound, while the characters still fear the worst. The same irony runs through the book, as when Tobit praises the trustworthy stranger who is really an angel (10:6).

a: Then people will laugh at us and mock us
p: In a culture of honor and shame, an eighth dead bridegroom would disgrace the whole family.
b: Sarah had already been taunted as the killer of her husbands (3:7–9). Raguel fears that another death will make the family a laughingstock. Ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern families lived by public honor; a hidden burial at night (8:12) would spare them shame. Biblical laments speak of public disgrace in the same way: "We have become a disgrace to our neighbors" (Psalm 79:4; compare Psalm 44:13–14).

a: sleeping peacefully, side by side
p: The Greek "together" (koinōs) repeats the end of Tobias's prayer. They prayed to grow old together, and they wake together.
b: Sinaiticus says the maid found them "sleeping and slumbering koinōs," the same adverb that closes the prayer in 8:7. The storyteller lets the word show the answer before anyone says it. Vaticanus just says she "found the two sleeping." The quiet scene contrasts with the grave outside.
orig: καθεύδοντας καὶ ὑπνοῦντας κοινῶς (katheudontas kai hypnountas koinōs)

a: two only children
p: Tobias and Sarah are each an only child. The same Greek word is used of Jesus in John.
b: Monogenēs means "one of a kind, only (child)." Sarah is her father's only child (3:15) and Tobias his parents' only son (6:15), which is why every death or delay threatens two families at once. The Greek Bible uses the word for Jephthah's daughter (Judges 11:34) and the widow's son at Nain (Luke 7:12), and John uses it of Jesus, God's "only" Son (John 1:14; John 3:16). In Tobit it carries the weight of a family's whole future.
orig: δύο μονογενεῖς (dyo monogeneis)

a: For fourteen days
p: Seven days was the usual wedding feast. Raguel doubles it.
b: Laban's wedding week for Jacob (Genesis 29:22, 27) and Samson's seven-day feast (Judges 14:12, 17) show the usual length of a wedding celebration. Raguel binds Tobias with an oath to stay fourteen (9:3; 10:7), a sign of his joy and his wealth. That oath is why Raphael must travel to Rages alone, and why Tobit and Anna wait in fear (10:1–7). The shorter Greek says Raguel spoke "under oath" here; Sinaiticus first mentions the oath in 9:3. Back in Nineveh a second, seven-day feast follows (11:19).

a: Take half of all I have right now
p: Raguel has no son, so his daughter's husband inherits everything: half now and half later.
b: The law let daughters inherit when there was no son (Numbers 27:8), and required such heiresses to marry within their tribe (Numbers 36:8). Raguel gives half his property at the wedding and promises the rest at his death. 10:10 lists the gift, and 14:13 says Tobias did inherit Raguel's household. The arrangement shows why the book cares about marriage within the family: land and goods stay with God's people even in exile.

a: the handwritten document
p: The document is the signed receipt for the money Tobit left with Gabael years before.
b: Tobit had left ten talents of silver in trust with Gabael (1:14), and gave Tobias the bond to collect it (4:20–5:3). The Greek cheirographon, "handwriting," means a signed document of debt or deposit, often written in two copies; 5:3 describes it as "a document in his own hand," and the Plain keeps that sense here. Paul uses the same word in Colossians 2:14, where God cancels "the record of debt" against us, nailing it to the cross. In Tobit the bond works: twenty years later Gabael pays in full.
orig: τὸ χειρόγραφον (to cheirographon)

a: You see the oath Raguel has sworn
t: An oath Sinaiticus did not mention
p: Sinaiticus never told us Raguel swore an oath. The shorter Greek says so in 8:20.
b: In Vaticanus, Raguel speaks to Tobias "under oath" (enorkōs) in 8:20. Sinaiticus has no oath there, but here and in 10:7 it speaks of "the oath Raguel has sworn." The longer text often assumes details it does not state. Either way the oath matters: Tobias will not break it even to spare his father worry, and a son's duty to keep his word stands beside his duty to his parents (Numbers 30:2).

a: their seals unbroken
t: A trust kept for twenty years
p: Gabael returns the sealed bags untouched: a picture of an honest steward.
b: The Greek says Gabael counted out the bags "with their seals." Money was stored in sealed bags so that anyone could see it had not been opened (2 Kings 12:10; Job 14:17). Tobit had left it long before (1:14; 5:3). In a book about faithfulness, Gabael is the faithful steward, who returns what was entrusted to him in full, as Jesus' parables praise (Luke 16:10–12).

a: righteous and a giver of alms
p: Gabael repeats what Raguel said in 7:7: Tobit is known for righteousness and alms.
b: Everyone who meets Tobias praises his father in the same words: "fine and good," "righteous," one who gives alms (7:7; 9:6). The Greek kalos kai agathos, "fine and good," was the Greek phrase for a true gentleman. Tobit's reputation travels farther than he can; the book's readers are meant to see the reward of a faithful life in the honor it brings to one's children (Proverbs 22:1; Sirach 3:11).
orig: Καλὲ καὶ ἀγαθέ, ἀνδρὸς καλοῦ καὶ ἀγαθοῦ, δικαίου καὶ ἐλεημοποιοῦ (kale kai agathe, andros kalou kai agathou, dikaiou kai eleēmopoiou)

a: you, the light of my eyes
p: Anna calls her son the light of her eyes; for a blind father, that is almost literally true.
b: "The light of my eyes" is a Hebrew way to speak of what gives one life and joy (Psalm 38:10). Tobit is blind, and Tobias has been his guide and hope. Anna's phrase prepares for 11:14, where Tobit, seeing again, greets his son with the same words. Light runs through these chapters: Tobit will "see the light" (11:8), and Ahiqar "came out into the light" (14:10).

a: The man traveling with him can be trusted
p: Tobit comforts Anna with words that are truer than he knows.
b: Tobit says the guide is trustworthy and "one of our own relatives." The reader knows he is the angel Raphael. The storyteller enjoys such double meanings, and they carry the book's message: God's help is present before anyone can see it. Readers in exile, who could not see God acting, were invited to trust as Tobit does here, while Anna's grief is treated with sympathy, not scorn.

a: I am sending messengers
p: The Greek word for Raguel's "messengers" is the same word as "angels."
b: Angelos means "messenger," human or heavenly. Raguel offers to send human messengers to Tobit; the reader knows that a heavenly messenger is already with Tobias. In the Bible the word must be read by context, as in Malachi 3:1 ("my messenger"), Luke 7:24 (John's messengers) and Revelation 1:20 (the "angels" of the seven churches).
orig: ἀποστέλλω ἀγγέλους (apostellō angelous)

a: I hand my daughter over to you for safekeeping
p: Edna gives her daughter to Tobias as a "deposit," the word for money held in trust.
b: Edna uses banking words: paratithemai and parathēkē mean to deposit something with a trusted person who must return it safely. The book began with Tobit's money deposited with Gabael (1:14); now a mother entrusts her daughter, a far greater treasure. Paul uses parathēkē for the gospel entrusted to Timothy and for what Paul has entrusted to God (1 Timothy 6:20; 2 Timothy 1:12, 14).
orig: παρατίθεμαί σοι τὴν θυγατέρα μου ἐν παραθήκῃ (paratithemai soi tēn thygatera mou en parathēkē)

a: He said to him
p: The Sinaiticus Greek says only "he said to him." The line may be damaged.
b: After Tobias leaves blessing God, the Greek has kai eipen autō, "and he said to him," then a wish that he may honor "them" all their days. It could be Raguel's last word to Tobias about honoring his new parents, or the end of a line in which Tobias blesses Raguel and Edna, as the shorter Greek has at 11:1 ("he kept blessing Raguel and Edna his wife"). Several editors think words have dropped out here. The Plain keeps the bare "he said to him."
orig: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ Εὐοδωθῇ σοι τιμᾷν αὐτοὺς (kai eipen autō, Euodōthē soi timan autous)

a: Kaserin
p: Only Sinaiticus names Kaserin, and no one has identified it.
b: The Greek is Kaserein, "opposite Nineveh." It may have been a town across the Tigris from Nineveh on the road from Media, but the name appears nowhere else, and scholars have offered only guesses. The shorter Greek gives no place name at all and says simply that Tobias traveled until he came near Nineveh.
orig: Κασερείν, ἥ ἐστιν κατέναντι Νινευή (Kaserein, hē estin katenanti Nineuē)

a: She spotted him on his way
p: Anna, like the father in Jesus' parable, sees her son coming from far off.
b: Anna has watched the road every day (10:7; 11:5). Many readers compare the father in the parable of the lost son, who sees his son "while he was still a long way off" and runs to him (Luke 15:20). Both stories turn a parent's grief into a homecoming feast (11:19; Luke 15:23–24). There is no sign that Luke borrowed from Tobit; the scene shows how naturally Jews pictured God's mercy as a parent's welcome.

a: I am sure his eyes will be opened
p: Tobit is healed by medicine that an angel teaches. The Bible elsewhere honors both God's power and physicians.
b: Agrees: Isaiah 35:5 promises that blind eyes will be opened, and Jesus' healings fulfill it (Matthew 11:5). Jesus sometimes uses means, such as mud and spit (John 9:6–7; Mark 8:23). Isaiah prescribes a fig poultice for Hezekiah's boil (Isaiah 38:21), and Sirach 38:1–15 says the Lord created medicines from the earth and gives skill to doctors. Differs in emphasis: Tobit gives detailed remedies (6:4–9) revealed by an angel, something the 66 books never do. Churches that read Tobit see in it God's healing through ordinary means.

a: the white films
t: Leukōmata, white films on the eyes
p: The Greek word means white patches on the cornea. Ancient doctors treated them with salves, some made with animal gall.
b: Tobit's blindness began when bird droppings fell into his eyes and left white films (2:10; 3:17). The Greek leukōmata is a medical word for white scars on the cornea; doctors still speak of a corneal "leukoma." Greek and Roman medicine used animal gall in eye salves, and Pliny the Elder's Natural History (32.24 in the Bostock–Riley translation) recommends the gall of the callionymus, a sea fish, for scars on the eyes. The story is told in terms its readers' doctors would recognize.
orig: ἀπολεπίσει τὰ λευκώματα (apolepisei ta leukōmata)

a: From now on I can die
p: Anna's words echo Jacob's when he saw Joseph alive in Egypt.
b: When Jacob met the son he had thought dead, he said, "I can die now" (Genesis 46:30). Anna had mourned Tobias as dead (10:4, 10:7), and she answers with the same joy. Simeon's song when he sees the child Jesus has the same shape: "now you are letting your servant go in peace" (Luke 2:29–30).

a: He blew into his eyes
p: The verb is the one Genesis uses for God breathing life into Adam.
b: Sinaiticus says Tobias "blew into" (enephysēsen) his father's eyes. The Greek Genesis uses the same verb when God breathes life into the first man (Genesis 2:7), and John uses it when the risen Jesus breathes on his disciples (John 20:22). Tobias may simply be blowing away the gall's sting, but the word gives the healing a sense of new creation. The shorter Greek says only that he sprinkled the gall on his eyes.
orig: ἐνεφύσησεν εἰς τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτοῦ (enephysēsen eis tous ophthalmous autou)

a: it began to work
p: Sinaiticus ends the verse with one word, epedōken. It probably means the medicine took hold.
b: The last word of the verse, epedōken, can mean "he applied it" or, used of a thing, "it went on, it took effect." The Plain takes the second sense, which leads straight into 11:12, where the shorter Greek says his eyes stung and he rubbed them. Sinaiticus as printed by Swete has no separate 11:12; see the entry on that verse.
orig: καὶ ἐπέβαλεν τὸ φάρμακον ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν καὶ ἐπέδωκεν (kai epebalen to pharmakon ep' auton kai epedōken)

a: blessed be all his holy angels
p: Tobit blesses God and also the angels. The 66 books have angels bless God, but people never bless angels.
b: Agrees: the Psalms call on the angels to bless the LORD (Psalm 103:20–21; Psalm 148:2). Goes beyond: Tobit's "blessed be all his holy angels" praises the angels themselves, and only after praising God. Jews of this period honored angels as God's servants, and later Jewish and Christian prayer kept such praise. Limit: in Revelation an angel refuses worship: "Worship God!" (Revelation 22:9), and Raphael himself tells Tobit and Tobias to bless God, not him (12:17–18). Catholic and Orthodox teaching honors angels but worships God alone. Reformed and many other Protestants hold that praise belongs to God alone, though Anglicans and Lutherans keep the feast of St Michael and All Angels (29 September).

a: He struck me
p: The verb means to whip or flog. Tobit's song in chapter 13 builds on it.
b: Tobit says God "whipped" him (emastigōsen) and now lets him see. The same verb and its noun run through his hymn: God "strikes, and he shows mercy" (13:2), he "will strike you for your wrongs" (13:5), and "the blows" on Jerusalem will end in joy (13:9, 13:14). The thought comes from Deuteronomy, "I strike down, and I make well" (Deuteronomy 32:39), and Proverbs 3:11–12, which the letter to the Hebrews quotes in its Greek form: the Lord "whips every son he receives" (Hebrews 12:6). Tobit reads his suffering as a father's discipline.
orig: αὐτὸς ἐμαστίγωσέν με (autos emastigōsen me)

a: all the Jews in Nineveh
p: Tobit's family is from Naphtali, yet the book calls the exiles "Jews."
b: Strictly, Ioudaioi means people of Judah, the southern kingdom. By the time Tobit was written, "Jew" had become the common name for all Israelites, as it is in Esther (Esther 3:6) and later writers. The word shows the book's real setting: it speaks to Jews of its own day, not to the eighth century BC it describes.
orig: πᾶσιν τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν Νινευή (pasin tois Ioudaiois tois ousin en Nineuē)

a: Ahiqar and Nadab, his nephews
p: Ahiqar was a famous sage of Assyrian legend. Tobit makes him Tobit's nephew and brings him to the party.
b: The Greek exadelphoi can mean cousins or nephews; 1:22 calls Ahiqar Tobit's nephew. Sinaiticus spells the second name Nabad here but Nadab in 14:10; Vaticanus has Nasbas, and the Aramaic story of Ahiqar calls Ahiqar's nephew Nadin. The Plain uses Nadab throughout. Ahiqar's betrayal by Nadab, told in 14:10, is the book's closing example of how God rescues the generous.
orig: Ἀχεικὰρ καὶ Ναβὰδ οἱ ἐξάδελφοι αὐτοῦ (Acheikar kai Nabad hoi exadelphoi autou)

a: make sure the man who traveled with you gets his pay
p: Tobit pays a hired man in full and adds a bonus, as the law and his own teaching require.
b: The law says not to hold back a worker's wages (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15), and Tobit had taught Tobias the same (4:14). Tobit had hired "Azariah" for a drachma a day plus expenses (5:15). Now father and son offer him half of everything. The scene sets up the surprise: the hired man is an angel who takes no pay (12:18).

a: thank him
p: The key verb of chapters 12–14 means to acknowledge God openly, to confess and give thanks in public.
b: Exomologeisthai is often "give thanks" or "praise," but it also means to declare openly, to confess. Raphael tells the family to thank God "before everyone alive" (12:6), and Tobit's hymn calls Israel to thank God "in front of the nations" (13:3). The book itself is the result: a public account of God's deeds (12:20). Jesus uses the verb, "I thank you, Father" (Matthew 11:25), and Paul for every tongue "confessing" Jesus as Lord (Philippians 2:11). The Plain uses "thank" and "give thanks" throughout these chapters.
orig: αὐτῷ ἐξομολογεῖσθε ἐνώπιον πάντων τῶν ζώντων (autō exomologeisthe enōpion pantōn tōn zōntōn)

a: A king's secret is best kept hidden
t: A king's secret and God's works
p: A wise saying with a twist: a king's plans are kept secret, but God's deeds should be told.
b: Raphael quotes a proverb and repeats it in 12:11. Proverbs 25:2 says that it is God's glory to hide a matter and kings' glory to search one out. Tobit turns it around: the king keeps his secret, but God's works must be revealed. There is also irony: Raphael has kept his own secret, and now he is about to reveal it (12:15). Sayings like this were common in Near Eastern wisdom, including the sayings of Ahiqar.

a: Giving alms is better than storing up gold
p: Raphael's saying anticipates Jesus' teaching about where to store treasure.
b: Tobit had taught Tobias that giving alms stores up "a good treasure" against the day of need (4:9). Raphael repeats it. Sirach says the same: "store up almsgiving in your storehouses" (Sirach 29:12). Jesus teaches, "pile up treasures for yourselves in heaven" (Matthew 6:19–21), and "sell your possessions and give alms" (Luke 12:33). The prayer, fasting and almsgiving of Matthew 6:1–18 match the triad of the shorter Greek of this verse (see the variant).

a: Alms rescue from death, and they cleanse away every sin
p: Raphael repeats Tobit's teaching of 4:10 and goes further: alms "cleanse away every sin." Here the churches part ways.
b: Agrees in part: Proverbs says "righteousness delivers from death" (Proverbs 10:2; Proverbs 11:4), and by Tobit's time Hebrew tsedaqah, "righteousness," also meant charity. Daniel urges a king to "break off" his sins by showing mercy to the poor (Daniel 4:27), Jesus says "give alms ... and everything will be clean for you" (Luke 11:41), and "love covers a multitude of sins" (1 Peter 4:8). Goes beyond, many say conflicts: 1 John 1:7 says it is Jesus' blood that "cleanses us from all sin," in very similar Greek. Catholic and Orthodox readers take Tobit to mean that mercy shown in God's grace heals sin's effects and obtains mercy; Lutheran and Reformed readers deny that any work atones. The churches' views are set out in the card at 4:10.
orig: ἐλεημοσύνη ἐκ θαυάτου ῥύεται, καὶ αὐτὴ ἀποκαθαίρει πᾶσαν ἁμαρτίαν (eleēmosynē ek thanatou rhyetai, kai autē apokathairei pasan hamartian; Sinaiticus misspells thanatou)
r: 4:10; Proverbs 10:2; Proverbs 11:4; Daniel 4:27; Luke 11:41; 1 Peter 4:8; 1 John 1:7

a: will be filled with life
p: The Greek means a full life. Jerome's Latin says alms make one find mercy and "the everlasting way."
b: The Greek chortasthēsontai zōēs, "they will be filled (fed full) with life," most likely means a long and full life on earth, the reward Tobit himself receives (14:1–2). Jerome's Vulgate reads: "facit invenire misericordiam et viam æternam", which the Douay renders "maketh to find mercy and life everlasting." Through the Latin the verse became a text about eternal life in Catholic preaching on almsgiving.
orig: οἱ ποιοῦντες ἐλεημοσύνην χορτασθήσονται ζωῆς (hoi poiountes eleēmosynēn chortasthēsontai zōēs)

a: the memorial of your prayer
p: Raphael carried a "memorial" of their prayer before God, the same word Acts uses of Cornelius's prayers and alms.
b: Mnēmosynon is something that brings a person to mind. In the Greek Leviticus it translates azkarah, the "token portion" of an offering burned before the LORD (Leviticus 2:2). Prayer here is pictured as an offering an angel brings into God's presence. An angel tells Cornelius, "your prayers and your alms have gone up as a memorial before God" (Acts 10:4), and Revelation 8:3–4 shows an angel offering incense with the prayers of God's people. Whether angels bring our prayers to God is the subject of the card at 1 Enoch 99.
orig: ἐγὼ προσήγαγον τὸ μνημόσυνον τῆς προσευχῆς ὑμῶν ἐνώπιον τῆς δόξης Κυρίου (egō prosēgagon to mnēmosynon tēs proseuchēs hymōn enōpion tēs doxēs Kyriou)

a: wrapped the dead man for burial
t: The burial that cost Tobit his sight
p: Raphael recalls the night in 2:3–8 when Tobit left his Pentecost dinner to bury a murdered man.
b: The verb periestelles means to wrap or lay out a body. Tobit buried the executed and the abandoned at the risk of his life (1:17–19; 2:3–8), and after that burial he went blind (2:9–10). Raphael now says that God saw every one of those deeds. Christian tradition counts burying the dead among the works of mercy largely because of Tobit; see the card at chapter 2.

a: put you to the test
p: Raphael says he was sent "to test" Tobit. The shorter Greek lacks the line, and the Vulgate makes it famous.
b: The verb peirasai, "to test," recalls "God put Abraham to the test" (Genesis 22:1) and the testing of Job. It does not say Raphael caused Tobit's blindness, but it reads the suffering as a trial within God's care. Jerome's Latin puts it memorably: "quia acceptus eras Deo, necesse fuit ut tentatio probaret te", "because thou wast acceptable to God, it was necessary that temptation should prove thee" (Douay 12:13). James 1:13 says God tempts no one to sin; testing that proves faith is another matter (James 1:2–3; 1 Peter 1:6–7).
orig: ἀπέσταλμαι ἐπὶ σὲ πειράσαι σε (apestalmai epi se peirasai se)

a: I am Raphael
p: Raphael means "God heals." The false name he gave, Azariah son of Hananiah, means "the LORD helps, son of the LORD is gracious."
b: The Hebrew name Rafa'el means "God has healed," and he has just healed Tobit and freed Sarah (12:14). In 5:13 he called himself "Azariah, son of the great Hananiah," names meaning "the LORD has helped" and "the LORD has been gracious." Many readers, ancient and modern, think the false name was chosen because it told the truth in a hidden way. Whether an angel may say what is not literally true is the subject of this chapter's card.
orig: Ῥαφαήλ (Rhaphaēl), Hebrew רְפָאֵל (Rafa'el), 'God has healed'

a: one of the seven angels who stand in attendance
p: Raphael is one of seven angels who serve in God's presence. Revelation also knows "the seven angels who stand in front of God."
b: Agrees: John sees "the seven angels who stand in front of God" (Revelation 8:2), and Gabriel tells Zechariah he "stands in the presence of God" (Luke 1:19). Ezekiel 9:2 has seven figures, one with a writing case, and Zechariah 4:10 speaks of seven eyes of the LORD. Goes beyond: the 66 books name only two angels, Michael and Gabriel; Tobit adds Raphael and the group of seven, as 1 Enoch 20 does with its list of seven archangels. Catholic and Orthodox churches honor Raphael by name (feast of 29 September in the Roman calendar); whether to honor angels named outside the 66 books is the card at 1 Enoch 20.
orig: εἷς τῶν ἑπτὰ ἀγγέλων οἳ παρεστήκασιν καὶ εἰσπορεύονται ἐνώπιον τῆς δόξης Κυρίου (heis tōn hepta angelōn hoi parestēkasin kai eisporeuontai enōpion tēs doxēs Kyriou)

a: they fell on their faces in fear
p: Tobit and Tobias react as Manoah, Daniel and Zechariah did when an angel was revealed.
b: Manoah and his wife fell face down when the angel went up in the altar's flame (Judges 13:20); Daniel fell on his face before Gabriel (Daniel 8:17); Zechariah was terrified (Luke 1:12). In Revelation John falls down to worship an angel and is told, "Worship God!" (Revelation 22:8–9). Raphael answers the same way: do not be afraid, and bless God (12:17–18).

a: Peace be with you
t: "Do not be afraid. Peace be with you."
p: Raphael's greeting is the one Gideon's angel gave, and the one the risen Jesus gave his disciples.
b: When Gideon feared he would die for seeing the angel of the LORD, the LORD said, "Peace to you; do not be afraid" (Judges 6:23). The risen Jesus greets the frightened disciples with "Peace be with you" (Luke 24:36; John 20:19). In each case a heavenly visitor calms the fear that his appearance causes, so that the hearers can listen.

a: Now you see that I never ate anything; you were seeing a vision
p: Raphael says he only seemed to eat. In Genesis the angels with Abraham do eat.
b: Differs: Abraham's visitors ate the meal he set before them (Genesis 18:8), and the angels in Sodom ate Lot's bread (Genesis 19:3). Agrees with the angel of Judges 13:16, who would not eat Manoah's food. Jewish interpreters such as Philo and Josephus later explained that Abraham's angels only appeared to eat (Josephus, Antiquities 1.197), as Tobit says here. The Vulgate expands the line: "I use an invisible meat and drink" (Douay 12:19). The risen Jesus does the opposite: he eats fish to prove he is not a ghost (Luke 24:41–43).

a: I am going up to the one who sent me
p: Raphael's farewell sounds like Jesus' words before his ascension.
b: "I am going to the one who sent me" is Jesus' phrase in John (John 7:33; John 16:5). Raphael then "went up" and was seen no more (12:21), as the angel of Judges 13:20 went up in the flame and Jesus was taken up and hidden by a cloud (Acts 1:9). The pattern of a divine messenger who comes, works unseen, reveals himself and departs was familiar to the first readers of the Gospels.

a: Put in writing everything that has happened to you
p: The angel orders the story written down. The book presents itself as that record.
b: Tobit begins "This is the book of the story of Tobit" (1:1) and is told in the first person through 3:6. The angel's command explains why such a book exists, as God tells Moses to write a record (Exodus 17:14) and Jeremiah to write his words in a book (Jeremiah 30:2), and Jesus tells John to write what he sees (Revelation 1:11). Catholic and Orthodox readers take this as the book's own account of its origin, while allowing for its literary form. Historical critics see a literary device: a Jewish author of the 200s BC presents his story as an old record, much as Daniel and 1 Enoch do.

a: Blessed be God, who lives forever
t: Tobit's hymn and the Dead Sea Scrolls
p: Some once thought chapters 13–14 were added later. The Qumran copies show the hymn was there by about 100 BC.
b: Chapter 13 is a psalm in two parts: praise of God who punishes and gathers his scattered people (13:1–8), and a song to Jerusalem rebuilt (13:9–18). Older scholars suggested it was a later addition. Aramaic and Hebrew fragments of Tobit from Qumran include parts of chapters 13 and 14, as reported by Fitzmyer, so the hymn belonged to the book in its oldest known copies, written in the first century BC.

a: He brings down to Hades
t: He brings down and brings up
p: Tobit's first lines draw on Hannah's song and the Song of Moses.
b: Hannah sang that the LORD "takes down to Sheol, and he brings up" (1 Samuel 2:6), and Moses' song says, "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). The Greek Hadēs stands for Hebrew She'ol, the world of the dead. Tobit applies the words to his own life (blindness and sight) and to Israel's (exile and return, 13:5). The Wisdom of Solomon uses the same line (Wisdom of Solomon 16:13), and Revelation gives the keys of Hades to Christ (Revelation 1:18).
orig: κατάγει ἕως ᾅδου κατωτάτω τῆς γῆς καὶ αὐτὸς ἀνάγει (katagei heōs hadou katōtatō tēs gēs kai autos anagei)
r: 1 Samuel 2:6; Deuteronomy 32:39; Revelation 1:18; Wisdom of Solomon 16:13

a: the great destruction
p: "The great destruction" is a name for the depths of the world of the dead, like Hebrew Abaddon.
b: The Greek apōleia is the word the Greek Bible often uses for Hebrew 'abaddon, "destruction," a poetic name for the place of the dead beside Sheol (Job 26:6; Job 28:22; Proverbs 15:11). Revelation names the angel of the abyss Abaddon, in Greek Apollyon, "Destroyer" (Revelation 9:11). Shorter Vaticanus has only "he brings down to Hades and brings up."
orig: ἐκ τῆς ἀπωλείας τῆς μεγάλης (ek tēs apōleias tēs megalēs)

a: for he has scattered you among them
t: Exile as a place of witness
p: Tobit tells exiles that God scattered them, and that among the nations they can make him known.
b: Tobit takes the hard view of the prophets that exile is God's punishment (13:5; Deuteronomy 28:64), but he adds a purpose: "there he has shown you his greatness," so Israel should praise him "in front of the nations." Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon (Jeremiah 29:7), and Isaiah calls Israel a light to the nations (Isaiah 49:6). For Jews living in the diaspora around 200 BC, this turned a life far from the land into a calling. Early Christians, scattered among the nations, read their own situation the same way (1 Peter 1:1; 1 Peter 2:12).

a: he is our Father
p: Tobit calls God "our Father," a title the Old Testament uses rarely and Jesus makes central.
b: Agrees: the Old Testament calls God Israel's Father in a few places (Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16; Isaiah 64:8; Malachi 2:10), and Jewish prayers of this period use the title more often (Sirach 23:1, 4). Jesus teaches his disciples to pray "Our Father" (Matthew 6:9). Tobit stands between the two: a diaspora Jew of the 200s BC confessing God as "our Lord, our God, our Father." Nothing here goes beyond the 66 books.

a: He will strike you for your wrongs
p: Tobit's hope follows Deuteronomy 30: exile for sin, then mercy and gathering when Israel turns back.
b: Deuteronomy 30:1–5 promises that when the scattered people turn back, "the LORD your God will turn back your captivity and show you compassion" (Deuteronomy 30:3) and gather them from the peoples. Tobit's hymn follows that order: strike, show mercy, gather (13:5), on condition of turning back (13:6). Sinaiticus says only that God will "have mercy on you all out of all the nations"; Vaticanus adds "and gather us."

a: with all your heart and all your being
t: Turning back with heart and being
p: Tobit quotes the language of Deuteronomy's call to return to God.
b: Deuteronomy says the scattered will turn back "with all your heart and all your being" (Deuteronomy 30:2), the same pair as the great command to love God (Deuteronomy 6:5). The Greek psychē here stands for Hebrew nefesh, which the site renders "being" in this phrase. Tobit adds a promise from the Psalms and prophets: God will no longer hide his face (Psalm 27:9; Isaiah 54:8; Ezekiel 39:29).

a: who knows whether he will want you and show you mercy
p: The line echoes the hope of Jonah's Nineveh and of Joel. The word for mercy is the word for alms.
b: "Who knows?" is the cautious hope of the king of Nineveh (Jonah 3:9) and of Joel (Joel 2:14): God is free, but merciful. The Greek word for God's mercy here is eleēmosynē, the same word that means "alms" elsewhere in Tobit. Human almsgiving imitates God's own mercy; the word joins the two.
orig: τίς γινώσκει εἰ θελήσει ὑμᾶς καὶ ποιήσει ἐλεημοσύνην ὑμῖν (tis ginōskei ei thelēsei hymas kai poiēsei eleēmosynēn hymin)

a: your tent will be built again in you with joy
p: "Tent" is the sanctuary, the Temple. Revelation uses the same word for God's home among people.
b: The Greek skēnē, "tent," recalls the tabernacle in the wilderness and becomes a name for the Temple (Psalm 27:5; Psalm 76:2). Amos promised that God would rebuild "the fallen booth of David" (Amos 9:11), which James applies to the church (Acts 15:16). Revelation uses skēnē for the final dwelling of God: "God's home is now with people" (Revelation 21:3). Sinaiticus says "your tent," Vaticanus "his tent," both meaning the house of God in Jerusalem.
orig: ἡ σκηνή σου οἰκοδομηθήσεταί σοι μετὰ χαρᾶς (hē skēnē sou oikodomēthēsetai soi meta charas)

a: A brilliant light will shine out to every corner of the earth
p: Tobit sings Isaiah 60's vision: light over Jerusalem, and the nations bringing gifts.
b: Isaiah 60 says "Arise, shine, for your light has come," and the nations come to that light carrying wealth (Isaiah 60:1–11; compare Isaiah 2:2–3; Psalm 72:10). Tobit repeats it for exiles who still wait. Revelation draws on the same chapter of Isaiah for the new Jerusalem: "The nations will walk by its light" (Revelation 21:24), and "They will bring the glory and honor of the nations into it" (Revelation 21:26). Christians have also seen it in the Magi's gifts (Matthew 2:11).

a: the name of the chosen city
p: The Greek word is feminine, so the Plain writes "the chosen city." The line has no verb in Greek.
b: Eklektē, "chosen," is feminine and refers to Jerusalem, the city God chose for his name (Deuteronomy 12:5; 1 Kings 11:13; Psalm 132:13). 2 John 1 greets "the chosen lady," probably a church, using the same word.
orig: ὄνομα τῆς ἐκλεκτῆς (onoma tēs eklektēs)

a: A curse on all who speak harsh words!
p: God's promise to Abraham, to bless those who bless him and curse those who curse him, is applied to Jerusalem.
b: God told Abraham, "I will bless those who bless you" and curse whoever curses him (Genesis 12:3; compare Numbers 24:9). Tobit gives Jerusalem the same protection: a curse on those who destroy it, a blessing on those who fear it. The list (walls, towers, houses burned) recalls the Babylonian destruction of 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9–10). Vaticanus has a shorter form: "Cursed are all who hate you; blessed forever are all who love you."

a: Happy are all people who grieve over you
p: Tobit echoes Isaiah 66:10: rejoice with Jerusalem, all you who mourned over her.
b: Isaiah 66:10 calls those who love Jerusalem and mourn over her to rejoice with her. Psalm 122:6 prays that those who love her may prosper. Tobit's "Happy" (makarioi, the word of Jesus' beatitudes) promises comfort to those who share Zion's grief, as Jesus' "Blessed are the mourners, because they will be comforted" (Matthew 5:4) does to a wider circle. Jewish tradition still comforts mourners as "among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem."
orig: μακάριοι πάντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι οἳ ἐπὶ σοὶ λυπηθήσονται (makarioi pantes hoi anthrōpoi hoi epi soi lypēthēsontai)

a: My soul blesses the Lord, the great King
p: The line joins Psalm 103:1 to the title "the great King" of Psalm 48.
b: "Bless the LORD, my soul" opens Psalms 103 and 104. God is "a great King over the whole earth" in Psalm 47:2, and Zion is "the town of the great King" in Psalm 48:2, a phrase Jesus uses of Jerusalem (Matthew 5:35). Tobit turns from Israel's praise to his own before singing of the city.

a: Jerusalem's gates will be made of sapphire and emerald
p: Tobit's jeweled city stands between Isaiah 54 and Revelation 21. The likeness is close; the differences matter.
b: Isaiah promises foundations of sapphire, battlements of rubies and gates of jewels (Isaiah 54:11–12). Tobit adds gold towers, mosaic streets and gates that sing (13:16–18). Revelation 21 shows walls of jasper, foundations of twelve jewels including sapphire and emerald, a city of pure gold, and "The twelve gates were twelve pearls" (Revelation 21:21). Agrees: all three use gems for God's beauty and permanence. Differs: Tobit's city is earthly Jerusalem rebuilt, with God's house in it (13:16; 14:5); John's comes down from heaven and "I did not see a temple in the city" (Revelation 21:22). How Christians read the hope is the card on this chapter.

a: red gems and with stone of Ophir
p: The "red gems" are anthrax, a glowing red stone; Ophir was the Bible's land of fine gold.
b: Anthrax, "live coal," is the Greek name for a fiery red gem, probably garnet or ruby; it is a stone in the high priest's breastpiece in the Greek Exodus (Exodus 28:18). Soupheir is a Greek spelling of Ophir, the far country of gold in Solomon's day (1 Kings 9:28; 1 Kings 10:11; Job 28:16). Vaticanus adds beryl. The Vulgate has instead "white and clean stone."
orig: ἄνθρακι ψηφολογηθήσονται καὶ λίθῳ Σουφείρ (anthraki psēphologēthēsontai kai lithō Soupheir)

a: Hallelujah!
p: The houses of Jerusalem cry the Hebrew word Hallelujah, kept as it was in the Greek.
b: Hallelujah is Hebrew for "praise Yah," that is, praise the LORD. The site's Plain of the Psalms renders it "Praise the LORD!"; here, as in Revelation 19:1–6, the Greek keeps the Hebrew word itself, so the Plain does too. Tobit is one of the few books outside the Psalms where a city or a crowd shouts it, as the heavenly crowd does in Revelation, and in both it celebrates God's final victory.
orig: Ἁλληλουιά (Hallēlouia)

a: 112 years old
t: A long life as a reward
p: Tobit lives to 112 and Tobias to 117. In the book's world a long life shows God's blessing.
b: The ages differ between the Greek forms of the book (see the variants at 14:1, 14:2 and 14:14), but in each, father and son live long lives after their trials, like Job, who lived 140 years more (Job 42:16–17). Tobit dies "in peace," as God promised Abraham (Genesis 15:15). For the book's readers this is the visible reward of faithfulness and alms (12:9).

a: the things Nahum spoke
t: Nahum, the prophet of Nineveh's fall
p: Sinaiticus names Nahum, whose whole book is about Nineveh's fall. Vaticanus and the KJV name Jonah.
b: Nahum's oracle is titled "a pronouncement about Nineveh" (Nahum 1:1), and chapters 2–3 picture the city's capture. Zephaniah 2:13–15 also foretells it. Jonah announced that Nineveh would be overthrown in forty days (Jonah 3:4), but the city repented and was spared (Jonah 3:10), so in the 66 books Jonah's warning did not come true in Nineveh's fall. That is why most recent scholars think "Nahum" is the original reading and "Jonah" a change by copyists who knew Jonah better as the prophet to Nineveh. Josephus, too, connects Jonah with a prophecy of Nineveh's fall (Antiquities 9.214). See the variant.
orig: ἃ ἐλάλησεν Ναούμ (ha elalēsen Naoum)
r: Nahum 1:1; Nahum 2:8–10; Nahum 3:7; Zephaniah 2:13–15; Jonah 3:4; Jonah 3:10

a: it will fall on Assyria and Nineveh
p: Sinaiticus writes Athēr, probably Athur, an Aramaic name for Assyria.
b: The Greek Athēr is otherwise unknown. In 14:15 Sinaiticus uses Athoureia, and Aramaic writers called Assyria Athur. Most take Athēr as a short or garbled form of that name, which suits a book first written in Aramaic. The Plain renders it "Assyria."
orig: ἀπαντήσει ἐπὶ Ἀθὴρ καὶ Νινευή (apantēsei epi Athēr kai Nineuē)

a: Our kinsmen who live in the land of Israel will all be counted and taken captive from the good land
p: Tobit, living in the 700s BC, foretells the fall of Jerusalem and the return. How should that be read?
b: Tobit foretells Judah's exile, the Temple burned (2 Kings 25:9), a return and a lesser second Temple (14:5), and then a glorious future. Catholic and Orthodox readers take the book as inspired and read these lines as true words about Israel's history, while many of their scholars, following Catholic teaching on literary forms (Dei Verbum 12), also accept that the author may be writing after the events. Historical critics read 14:4–5 as "prophecy after the event": a writer around 200 BC tells, in Tobit's voice, history already past, so that readers will trust the part still to come (14:5b–7). The account says nothing of Antiochus IV's desecration of the Temple in 167 BC, a reason many date the book before it.

a: though it will not equal the first
p: Tobit knows that the rebuilt Temple of the 500s BC was humble compared with Solomon's.
b: Old men who had seen Solomon's Temple wept when the foundation of the new one was laid (Ezra 3:12), and Haggai asked who remembered the house "in its former glory" (Haggai 2:3). Tobit says this lesser house will last only "until the appointed times run their full course"; then Jerusalem and God's house will be rebuilt in glory. 1 Enoch 90:28–29 has the same hope of a new house. For Christians, Jesus speaks of the temple of his body (John 2:19–21), and Revelation's city needs no temple (Revelation 21:22).
r: Ezra 3:12; Haggai 2:3; Haggai 2:9; John 2:19–21; Revelation 21:22; 1 Enoch 90:28–29

a: All the nations in the whole world will turn and truly fear God
p: Tobit ends with the prophets' widest hope: all nations will abandon idols and worship Israel's God.
b: Isaiah sees the nations streaming to the LORD's mountain (Isaiah 2:2–4), Zechariah sees ten men of every language taking hold of a Jew's robe to go with him (Zechariah 8:20–23), and Zephaniah promises that the peoples will call on the LORD's name (Zephaniah 3:9). Tobit shares that open hope, even as he keeps a strict line about marriage. Paul's mission to the Gentiles grew from the same promises (Romans 15:9–12).

a: live securely for all time in Abraham's land
p: The gathered Israelites will live safely in the land promised to Abraham.
b: God gave the land to Abraham and his offspring (Genesis 15:18; Genesis 17:8). The prophets promised that the gathered people would "live in safety" there (Ezekiel 28:26; Jeremiah 23:6). Tobit adds "for all time," the hope of an everlasting inheritance. Christians differ on how such promises are fulfilled; see the cards on the promised land at Joshua 21 and Numbers 34.

a: Think, my child, about how Nadab treated Ahiqar
p: Ahiqar was the hero of an old Aramaic tale: a wise courtier betrayed by the nephew he raised.
b: A copy of The Words of Ahiqar was found among Aramaic papyri from Elephantine in Egypt, from the late 400s BC. In the Elephantine copy, Ahiqar, a counselor of the Assyrian kings Sennacherib and Esarhaddon, adopts his nephew Nadin (Tobit's Nadab), who slanders him. Ahiqar is condemned, but the officer sent to kill him hides him, because Ahiqar had once saved that officer's life. The papyrus breaks off there. Ahiqar's return to favor and Nadin's punishment are known from the later versions of the story, in Syriac, Armenian, Arabic and other languages. Tobit makes Ahiqar a member of his family (1:21–22) and uses his rescue as proof that mercy saves from death.

a: Was Ahiqar not put down into the earth while he was still alive?
p: Ahiqar went down into the earth and came back to the light; Nadab went into darkness forever.
b: In the tale Ahiqar was hidden in an underground chamber. Tobit turns the story into a picture of death and return: Ahiqar "came out into the light," while Nadab "went down into darkness forever." The language is close to Psalm 30:3 ("you lifted my life out of Sheol") and to the righteous rescued from the pit they were thrown into while the wicked fall into the pit they dug (Psalm 7:15; Psalm 57:6; Proverbs 26:27). Haman in Esther falls in the same way (Esther 7:10).

a: at what alms do, and at what wrongdoing does: it kills
p: Tobit's last words set two paths before his children, as Moses did: one leads to life, one to death.
b: Moses told Israel, "Life and death are what I have put before you, blessing and curse" (Deuteronomy 30:19), and Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous with the way of the wicked. Tobit's final lesson is the same, made concrete: alms save from death (12:9; 14:10), wrongdoing kills. Jesus' two ways (Matthew 7:13–14) and the early Christian Didache carry the pattern on.

a: the captives that Achiacharus king of Media had taken
p: Nineveh fell in 612 BC to the Medes under Cyaxares and the Babylonians under Nabopolassar.
b: The Babylonian Chronicle records that Nabopolassar of Babylon and the Median king Umakishtar (Greek Cyaxares) took Nineveh in 612 BC. Herodotus also says the Medes under Cyaxares captured it. The first hand of Sinaiticus calls the conqueror "Achiacharus king of Media"; this is probably a copyist's confusion of the rare name Cyaxares with Ahiqar's name, which Vaticanus spells the same way. A later corrector of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus have "Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus" instead. The Plain prints the Sinaiticus name and leaves the confusion visible; see the variant.
orig: ἣν ᾐχμαλώτισεν Ἀχιάχαρος ὁ βασιλεὺς τῆς Μηδίας (hēn ēchmalōtisen Achiacharos ho basileus tēs Mēdias)

a: he rejoiced over Nineveh
p: Tobias rejoices at Nineveh's destruction. Nahum agrees; Jonah shows God's pity for the same city.
b: Agrees: Nahum ends with everyone who hears of Nineveh's fall clapping their hands (Nahum 3:19), and Revelation calls heaven to rejoice over Babylon's fall (Revelation 18:20). Stands in tension with: Jonah ends with God's question, "Should I not care about Nineveh?" (Jonah 4:11), and Proverbs warns, "When your enemy falls, do not be glad" (Proverbs 24:17). Tobit's joy is not personal revenge but relief that the oppressor of God's people is judged, as the prophets foretold (14:4).
